owl.title: THIS BIRD HUNTS IN NEAR SILENCE
owl.script: An owl can turn its head up to 270 degrees without cutting off blood flow. Its eyes are so large and fixed in their sockets that it cannot roll them like we do, so the neck has to do the work. Extra space in the neck's blood vessels helps keep blood moving during extreme turns. Many owls also have asymmetrical ear openings, letting them compare tiny differences in sound and pinpoint prey in darkness. Their facial disc acts like a satellite dish, funneling sound toward the ears. And those almost silent wingbeats? Soft fringes on the feathers break up turbulence and reduce noise. By the time a mouse hears an owl coming, the attack may already be over.
owl.caption:
Owls are built to hunt in near silence. 🦉

shark.title: IT CAN FEEL ELECTRICITY
shark.script: A shark is basically a living sensory machine. Its skeleton is made of cartilage instead of bone, making the body lighter and flexible. Its skin is covered in tiny tooth-like scales called dermal denticles, which reduce drag as water moves across the body. Around the snout are special organs called the ampullae of Lorenzini. They can detect extremely weak electrical fields produced by the muscles and nerves of other animals, helping a shark locate prey even when visibility is poor. Sharks also replace teeth throughout their lives, with new rows moving forward as older teeth are lost. And their family line is ancient: shark ancestors were swimming in Earth's oceans long before the first true trees appeared on land.
shark.caption:
Sharks can detect the electrical signals of living animals. 🦈

chameleon.title: CAMOUFLAGE ISN'T THE WEIRDEST PART
chameleon.script: A chameleon's color change is not just about camouflage. In many species, shifting colors also helps control body temperature and communicate with rivals or potential mates. Beneath the skin are specialized cells containing tiny crystals that can change how light is reflected. Its eyes can move in different directions, letting it scan a huge area without moving its head, then work together when it locks onto prey. The feet are shaped like gripping tongs for holding branches, and many species use a prehensile tail as an extra anchor. Then comes the tongue. In some chameleons it can shoot farther than the animal's body length, accelerating incredibly fast and grabbing insects before they have time to react.
chameleon.caption:
A chameleon's color change is only the beginning. 🦎

frog.title: THIS ANIMAL DRINKS THROUGH ITS SKIN
frog.script: Frogs do not always drink water the way mammals do. Many absorb it directly through a specialized patch of skin on the belly and thighs. That skin also plays a major role in breathing, which is one reason frogs need to stay moist. Their tongue is attached near the front of the mouth, allowing it to flip outward rapidly and grab prey. Here is an even stranger trick: in many frogs, the eyes can retract downward while swallowing and help push food toward the throat. The round disk you may see behind the eye is the tympanum, an external eardrum used to detect sound. And some species have pushed survival even further, tolerating part of their body freezing during winter before becoming active again in spring.
frog.caption:
Frogs can absorb water directly through their skin. 🐸
